title: Student Loan Defaults Surge Past 9 Million as Post-Pandemic Repayment Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Nearly 3.6 million Americans defaulted on federal student loans in just six months. With wage garnishments resuming and the SAVE plan dead, millions more face a ticking clock.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 9.5 million federal student loan borrowers are in default, with totals expected to reach 12.5 million by year-end.
  • 3.6 million borrowers defaulted in just six months, many were current before the pandemic pause.
  • Wage garnishments have resumed, impacting borrowers' disposable income and credit scores significantly.
  • Average credit scores for newly defaulted borrowers dropped by 91 points, affecting their access to loans.

  • Nearly 9.6 million federal student loan borrowers were in default as of March 31, with another 3 million delinquent — totals that could reach 12.5 million by year's end.
  • About 3.6 million borrowers defaulted in just two quarters (Q4 2025 and Q1 2026), most of whom were current on their loans before the pandemic pause.
  • The Treasury Department has permanently resumed involuntary wage garnishments for defaulted borrowers, while 7.5 million former SAVE plan enrollees are being directed to choose new repayment options by October.
  • Credit scores for newly defaulted borrowers dropped an average of 91 points, effectively locking them out of mortgages, auto loans, and traditional credit for years.

The US student loan system is deep in crisis. Three years after the pandemic payment pause ended, the number of federal borrowers in default has climbed to 9.57 million — the highest recorded figure — with an additional 2.97 million delinquent, according to Department of Education data through March 31.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest Household Debt and Credit Report mapped the collapse across two brutal quarters. Roughly one million borrowers defaulted in the fourth quarter of 2025, and another 2.6 million followed in the first quarter of 2026. The share of student loan balances at least 90 days past due climbed to 10.3%, approaching levels not seen since before the pandemic suppressed delinquency rates.

A New Kind of Defaulter

What distinguishes this wave from earlier cycles is the profile of who is falling behind. According to the New York Fed's research, the average newly defaulted borrower is nearly 39 years old — 2.5 years older than the pre-pandemic average. Nearly 30% of recent defaulters were current on their loans before the pause. Close to half had not yet taken out loans or owed no payment at the time, due to grace periods, deferment, or income-driven repayment plans.

Only about 4% of borrowers in the current wave were already in default before the pandemic. "That breakdown reveals a new group struggling to restart payments, rather than a carryover of chronic nonpayment from earlier years," the New York Fed researchers wrote.

> **"Nearly 30% of recent defaulters were current on their loans before the pause."**

Geographically, states in the South are hardest hit. Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and South Carolina each have at least 10% of their student loan borrowers in default. But no state is immune — even the least-affected states have at least 4% of borrowers in default.

"Nearly 30% of recent defaulters were current on their loans before the pause."

The Government Tightens the Screws

The federal response has shifted from patience to enforcement. "Not paying your loans is no longer an option," Nicholas Kent, under secretary at the Department of Education, said earlier this year, according to Investopedia.

The Treasury Department has permanently resumed involuntary wage garnishments for defaulted borrowers — a process that can seize up to 15% of disposable income, along with tax refunds and Social Security payments. Credit scores for recently defaulted borrowers dropped an average of 91 points, from 567 to 476, according to the New York Fed, pushing most below thresholds required for mortgages or auto loans. The default notation remains on credit reports for seven years.

Newly defaulted borrowers are also struggling across their broader financial lives. The New York Fed found that nearly 40% of those with auto loans are past due, 56% of those with credit cards are delinquent, and 20% with mortgages have fallen behind.

SAVE Collapse Adds Fuel

Compounding the crisis is the end of the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) repayment plan. Introduced by the Biden administration in 2023 as the most affordable federal option, SAVE was blocked by courts in 2024 and permanently terminated in March 2026 after a settlement between the Trump administration and Missouri. Approximately 7.5 million borrowers spent nearly two years in forbearance while the legal fight played out.

Those borrowers are now receiving notices in July 2026 directing them to choose a new repayment plan within 90 days. The New York Fed warned that because very few of these borrowers have re-entered repayment since the plan was suspended, "a second wave of defaults might emerge as these 7 million borrowers reach the nine-month mark in the repayment period."

Two new federal repayment plans launched on July 1 to give borrowers alternatives. The income-driven Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) sets payments between 1% and 10% of earnings with a $10 monthly floor. The Tiered Standard Plan assigns fixed payments over 10 to 25 years based on total balance.

A Wider Burden for Indian Americans

The default crisis resonates across the Indian diaspora in the United States. Indian Americans who financed graduate or professional education with federal student loans face the same repayment pressures. Meanwhile, Indian students on F-1 visas, who typically rely on private loans with interest rates of 10% to 16%, are fast-tracking repayments amid visa and job uncertainties, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. Some are seeing education loans of $75,000 balloon past $100,000.

"Default is always more expensive, whether it be monthly or whether it be in the long term."

— Betsy Mayotte, President, The Institute of Student Loan Advice

What Comes Next

For borrowers already in default, two main paths lead back to good standing: loan rehabilitation, which requires nine on-time payments within 10 months, or a Direct Consolidation Loan, which typically takes four to six weeks, according to the National Consumer Law Center.

The Department of Education is also offering eligible borrowers a temporary 1-percentage-point interest rate reduction for signing up for autopay between July 1 and September 30. But experts remain cautious. Even as the New York Fed suggested the "largest wave of student loan defaults has passed," researchers warned the ripples will reverberate through family credit profiles and the broader economy when collections resume at full force.
